subject: science
title: More About the Solar System
bookChapter: Chapter 12: More About the Solar System

preamble.whatYouWillLearn: You will learn the order of the planets and how the planets, the Earth, the Moon and the Sun move. You will find out why the Moon seems to change shape over a month. You will also see how models and new evidence changed our ideas about the Solar System.
preamble.whyItMatters: The movements of the Earth and Moon give us our days, months and years. Understanding them explains sunrise, sunset and the changing Moon you see from your window. It also shows how science changes when new evidence is found.
realWorld: The Islamic calendar uses the new crescent moon to mark the start of each month, such as the start of Ramadan
Chinese families celebrate the Mid-Autumn Festival with mooncakes on the night of a full moon
When it is lunchtime in Kuala Lumpur, it is still early morning in London, because the Earth is spinning
The National Planetarium in Kuala Lumpur uses models to show the planets and their orbits
Leap years add 29 February to keep our calendar in step with the Earth's orbit

subtopics.title: The Sun and the planets
subtopics.summary: The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System. Eight planets orbit it: four rocky inner planets and four giant outer planets.

subtopics.title: Movements of the Earth, Moon and planets
subtopics.summary: The Earth spins once a day, giving day and night, and orbits the Sun once a year. The Moon orbits the Earth.

subtopics.title: Phases of the Moon
subtopics.summary: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits the Earth we see different amounts of the lit half, in a cycle of about 29 1/2 days.

subtopics.title: Models and changing ideas
subtopics.summary: Models help us understand the Solar System. Evidence changed the idea of an Earth-centred universe to a Sun-centred Solar System.

questions.prompt: What is at the centre of our Solar System?
options: The Earth
The Moon
The Sun
Jupiter
questions.solution: The Sun is a star at the centre of the Solar System. The eight planets, including Earth, all orbit (travel around) the Sun.

misconceptions.0: Long ago people thought the Earth was at the centre, because the Sun seems to move across our sky. We now know the Earth orbits the Sun.
misconceptions.1: The Moon orbits the Earth. It is much smaller than the Earth and is not at the centre of anything.
misconceptions.3: Jupiter is the biggest planet, but it orbits the Sun like all the other planets.

questions.prompt: Put these planets in order from closest to the Sun to furthest from the Sun.
options: Earth
Jupiter
Mercury
Mars
Venus
questions.solution: Going out from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, then Jupiter. A sentence can help you remember the order of all eight planets, for example 'My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming' (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune).

misconceptions.common: Swapping Mercury and Venus, or putting Mars before Earth. Earth is the third planet from the Sun and Mars is the fourth.

questions.prompt: Which is the largest planet in the Solar System?
options: Saturn
Jupiter
Earth
The Sun
questions.solution: Jupiter is the largest planet. It is a gas giant, about 11 times wider than the Earth. The Sun is bigger still, but it is a star, not a planet.

misconceptions.0: Saturn's huge rings make it look very big, and it is the second largest planet, but Jupiter is larger.
misconceptions.2: Earth feels big to us, but it is a small rocky planet. More than 1000 Earths could fit inside Jupiter.
misconceptions.3: The Sun is much bigger than Jupiter, but the Sun is a star, not a planet.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the planets that are rocky inner planets.
options: Venus
Jupiter
Mercury
Saturn
Mars
Earth
questions.solution: The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. The four outer planets are giants: Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants, and Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.

misconceptions.1: Jupiter is a gas giant, one of the four outer planets beyond the asteroid belt.
misconceptions.3: Saturn is a gas giant made mostly of gas, not rock. It is an outer planet.

questions.prompt: True or false: The Sun is a star.
questions.solution: True. The Sun is a star, a huge ball of very hot gas that gives out its own light and heat. It looks much bigger and brighter than the other stars only because it is much closer to us.

misconceptions.common: Thinking the Sun cannot be a star because stars look like tiny dots at night. The other stars look small only because they are much further away.

questions.prompt: Pluto used to be called the ninth planet. Why is it no longer called a planet?
options: Pluto was destroyed, so it no longer exists
Scientists found out that Pluto is a moon of Neptune
Pluto stopped orbiting the Sun
In 2006 scientists decided it is a dwarf planet, because it is small and shares its orbit with many other icy objects
questions.solution: As scientists discovered more icy objects beyond Neptune, they agreed on what counts as a planet. Pluto is small and has not cleared its orbit of other objects, so in 2006 it was classified as a dwarf planet. This is an example of scientific ideas changing when new evidence is found.

misconceptions.0: Pluto still exists and still orbits the Sun. Only its name group changed, from planet to dwarf planet.
misconceptions.1: Pluto orbits the Sun, not Neptune. It is a dwarf planet, not a moon.
misconceptions.2: Pluto still orbits the Sun. It takes about 248 years to go round once.

questions.prompt: Arjun predicts: 'The further a planet is from the Sun, the colder its surface.' He finds this table of average surface temperatures (planets listed in order from the Sun): Mercury 167 °C, Venus 464 °C, Earth 15 °C, Mars -65 °C. Which planet does NOT fit his prediction?
options: Mercury
Venus
Earth
Mars
questions.solution: If the prediction were right, the temperatures should go down as you move away from the Sun. Mercury should be hottest. But Venus, which is further away, is hotter (464 °C) than Mercury (167 °C). So Venus does not fit the prediction. Earth and Mars do fit.

misconceptions.0: Mercury is closest to the Sun, so the prediction says it should be the hottest of these four. But Venus is even hotter, so Venus is the one that breaks the pattern.
misconceptions.2: Earth (15 °C) is colder than Venus and warmer than Mars, so it fits the pattern.
misconceptions.3: -65 °C is the coldest temperature in the table (below zero), and Mars is the furthest away, so it fits the prediction.

questions.prompt: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun, but Venus has the hottest surface of all the planets. What is the best explanation?
options: Venus has a very thick atmosphere, mostly carbon dioxide, that traps the heat
Venus is closer to the Sun than Mercury
Venus is a gas giant, and gas giants are hotter
Venus makes its own light and heat, like the Sun
questions.solution: Mercury has almost no atmosphere, so its heat escapes into space. Venus is covered in a very thick atmosphere of carbon dioxide with clouds. This traps heat like a blanket, so Venus is hotter than Mercury even though it is further from the Sun.

misconceptions.1: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun. Venus is the second planet.
misconceptions.2: Venus is a small rocky planet. The gas giants (Jupiter and Saturn) are far from the Sun and very cold at their cloud tops.
misconceptions.3: Planets do not make their own light. Venus shines in our sky only because it reflects sunlight.

questions.prompt: Which planet is fourth from the Sun and is often called the Red Planet?
questions.solution: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, after Mercury, Venus and Earth. Its rocks and dust contain iron oxide (rust), which makes it look red.

misconceptions.common: Answering Jupiter. Jupiter is fifth from the Sun; Mars comes just before it.

questions.prompt: What causes day and night on Earth?
options: The Sun moves around the Earth once a day
The Earth spins on its axis, once about every 24 hours
The Earth orbits the Sun once a day
The Moon blocks the Sun's light every night
questions.solution: The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis once about every 24 hours. The side facing the Sun has day; the side facing away has night. As the Earth turns, places move from day into night and back again.

misconceptions.0: The Sun only seems to move across the sky. It is really the Earth turning that makes the Sun appear to rise and set.
misconceptions.2: One orbit of the Sun takes a whole year (about 365 1/4 days). Day and night come from the Earth spinning, not orbiting.
misconceptions.3: The Moon does not cause night. Night is when your side of the Earth has turned to face away from the Sun.

questions.prompt: How many days does it take the Earth to orbit the Sun once? Give your answer to the nearest whole day.
questions.solution: The Earth takes about 365 1/4 days to travel once around the Sun. To the nearest whole day that is 365 days, which is one year.

misconceptions.common: Answering 24 (hours), which is the time for the Earth to spin once, not to orbit the Sun.

questions.prompt: True or false: The Moon orbits the Earth, and the Earth orbits the Sun.
questions.solution: True. The Moon travels around the Earth, and at the same time the Earth (taking the Moon with it) travels around the Sun.

misconceptions.common: Thinking the Sun orbits the Earth because it seems to move across our sky.

questions.prompt: Match each movement to the time it takes.

left: The Earth spins once on its axis
The Earth orbits the Sun once
The Moon orbits the Earth once

questions.solution: The Earth spins once in about 24 hours (one day). It orbits the Sun once in about 365 1/4 days (one year). The Moon orbits the Earth once in about 27 to 28 days (about 27 1/3 days). (The Moon's phases repeat about every 29 1/2 days, a little longer, because the Earth has moved along its own orbit in that time.)

misconceptions.common: Mixing up spinning (a day) and orbiting (a year). A spin is turning on the spot; an orbit is a journey all the way around something.

questions.prompt: True or false: The Sun rises in the east and sets in the west because the Sun travels around the Earth every day.
questions.solution: False. The Sun does rise in the east and set in the west, but that is because the Earth spins from west to east. As your part of the Earth turns towards the Sun it looks like sunrise, and as it turns away it looks like sunset.

misconceptions.common: Believing what it looks like from the ground. It feels as if we are still and the Sun moves, but really the Earth is turning.

questions.prompt: The Earth takes about 365 1/4 days to orbit the Sun, but a normal calendar year has 365 days. Why do we add an extra day (29 February) every 4 years?
options: The Earth slows down every fourth year
The Moon takes an extra day to orbit the Earth every fourth year
Four extra quarter days add up to one whole day
To make February the same length as the other months
questions.solution: Each year the Earth needs about 1/4 of a day more than 365 days. After 4 years: 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 = 1 whole day. So every 4 years we add one day to keep the calendar in step with the Earth's orbit.

misconceptions.0: The Earth's speed does not change from year to year. The extra day is needed because of the 1/4 day left over each year.
misconceptions.1: The calendar year is based on the Earth orbiting the Sun, not on the Moon.
misconceptions.3: Even with 29 days, February is still shorter than every other month.

questions.prompt: A normal year has 365 days and a leap year has 366 days. How many days are there altogether in 4 years in a row, if exactly one of them is a leap year? Give your answer in days.
questions.solution: Three normal years: 3 x 365 = 1095 days. One leap year: 366 days. Total: 1095 + 366 = 1461 days. (This is the same as 4 x 365 1/4 = 1461.)

misconceptions.common: Doing 4 x 365 = 1460 and forgetting the extra leap day.

questions.prompt: From Earth, we always see the same side of the Moon. Which statement explains this?
options: The Moon does not spin at all
The Earth's shadow always covers the other side of the Moon
The Moon spins once on its axis in the same time that it takes to orbit the Earth once
The other side of the Moon never gets any sunlight
questions.solution: The Moon takes about 27 days to orbit the Earth, and it also takes about 27 days to spin once. Because these match, the same side always faces the Earth. Try it: walk around a chair while always facing it. You turn around once as you go around once.

misconceptions.0: If the Moon did not spin, we would see all of its sides as it travelled around the Earth. It does spin, exactly once per orbit.
misconceptions.1: The Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon during a lunar eclipse. It is not why we always see the same side.
misconceptions.3: The far side of the Moon gets sunlight too; at new moon it is fully lit. We just never see it from Earth.

questions.prompt: A table shows each planet's distance from the Sun and the time it takes to orbit the Sun once: Mercury 58 million km, 88 days; Venus 108 million km, 225 days; Earth 150 million km, 365 days; Mars 228 million km, 687 days. Which conclusion do these data support?
options: The closer a planet is to the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit the Sun once
All the planets take about the same time to orbit the Sun
Bigger planets take longer to orbit the Sun
The further a planet is from the Sun, the longer it takes to orbit the Sun once
questions.solution: Look at both columns together. As the distance goes up (58, 108, 150, 228 million km), the orbit time also goes up (88, 225, 365, 687 days). So the further a planet is from the Sun, the longer its year. A further planet has a longer path to travel and also moves more slowly.

misconceptions.0: This is the pattern back to front. Mercury is closest and takes only 88 days, the shortest time.
misconceptions.1: The times are very different, from 88 days to 687 days. Always check the numbers before choosing a conclusion.
misconceptions.2: The table does not give the sizes of the planets, so this conclusion is not supported by these data. (In fact Mars is smaller than Earth but takes longer.)

questions.prompt: Why can we see the Moon shining in the night sky?
options: It gives out its own light, like the Sun
It glows because it is very hot
It reflects light from the Sun
It reflects light from the stars
questions.solution: The Sun is a light source. The Moon is not; it reflects sunlight. Light from the Sun hits the Moon, bounces off and travels to our eyes, so we see it.

misconceptions.0: The Moon is not a light source. It is a ball of rock that we see only because sunlight bounces off it.
misconceptions.1: The Moon is not hot enough to glow. It shines only because it reflects sunlight.
misconceptions.3: Starlight is far too faint to light up the Moon. The Moon's light is reflected sunlight.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the phase when the whole side of the Moon facing the Earth is lit, so we see a complete bright circle?
questions.solution: This is a full moon. It happens when the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, so we see all of the Moon's lit half.

misconceptions.common: Answering 'new moon'. At new moon we see almost nothing, because the lit side faces away from us.

questions.skill: naming the phases of the Moon

questions.prompt: True or false: The phases of the Moon are caused by the Earth's shadow falling on the Moon.
questions.solution: False. Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half, which gives the phases. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon only during a lunar eclipse, which is rare.

misconceptions.common: This is one of the most common mistakes about the Moon. If the Earth's shadow caused the phases, the Moon would be hidden at full moon, but at full moon the Moon is fully lit.

questions.prompt: Starting from the new moon, put these phases of the Moon in the order they happen.
options: full moon
waxing crescent
waxing gibbous
new moon
first quarter
questions.solution: After a new moon, a thin waxing crescent appears. It grows to a first quarter (half of the face lit), then a waxing gibbous (more than half lit), and then a full moon. 'Waxing' means the lit part is getting bigger.

misconceptions.common: Putting waxing gibbous before first quarter. A crescent is less than half lit, a quarter is half lit and gibbous is more than half lit, so the order is crescent, quarter, gibbous.

questions.skill: naming the phases of the Moon

questions.prompt: What word describes the Moon when the lit part we can see is getting bigger each night? Answer in one word.
questions.solution: When the lit part is growing, the Moon is waxing. When it is shrinking after full moon, the Moon is waning.

misconceptions.common: Mixing up waxing (growing, from new moon to full moon) and waning (shrinking, from full moon to new moon).

questions.skill: naming the phases of the Moon

questions.prompt: About how long is it from one full moon to the next full moon?
options: About 7 days
About 29 1/2 days
About 24 hours
About 365 days
questions.solution: The Moon goes through all its phases, from full moon back to full moon, in about 29 1/2 days. That is about one month; the word 'month' comes from 'moon'.

misconceptions.0: About 7 days is the time between one main phase and the next, for example from new moon to first quarter. A full cycle takes about four times as long.
misconceptions.2: 24 hours is the time for the Earth to spin once. The Moon's cycle of phases takes about a month.
misconceptions.3: 365 days is the time for the Earth to orbit the Sun, one year. There are about 12 full moons in a year.

questions.prompt: At new moon we can hardly see the Moon at all. Where is the Moon at new moon?
options: Between the Earth and the Sun, so its lit side faces away from us
On the far side of the Earth from the Sun
Inside the Earth's shadow
Behind the Sun, where the Sun hides it
questions.solution: At new moon the Moon is roughly between the Earth and the Sun. The Sun lights the side of the Moon facing away from us, and the side facing us is dark, so we can hardly see it. It is also in the sky during the day, close to the bright Sun.

misconceptions.1: That is where the Moon is at full moon. Then the lit side faces us and we see a full circle.
misconceptions.2: The Moon is in the Earth's shadow only during a lunar eclipse. At new moon it is on the Sun's side of the Earth, not in our shadow.
misconceptions.3: The Moon orbits the Earth, so it never goes behind the Sun. At new moon it is between us and the Sun.

questions.prompt: Siti wants to find out how the Moon's appearance changes over a month. Which plan is best?
options: Draw the Moon on one night and copy that drawing for the other days
Draw the Moon only on the night of the full moon
Watch the Moon through a telescope for one hour on a single night
Draw the Moon's shape at about the same time every clear night for a month, writing the date each time
questions.solution: This is an 'observing over time' enquiry. The Moon's phases change slowly over about a month, so Siti needs regular observations: every clear night, about the same time, with the date recorded. If it is cloudy she can leave a gap and carry on the next night.

misconceptions.0: One observation cannot show a change. She must observe again and again over time.
misconceptions.1: That shows only one phase. To see how the Moon changes she needs to observe it on many nights through the month.
misconceptions.2: The Moon's shape changes very little in one hour. The phases change over days and weeks.

questions.prompt: Tonight the Moon is at first quarter. About how long will it be until the next full moon?
options: About 1 week
About 2 weeks
About 3 weeks
About 4 weeks
questions.solution: The whole cycle takes about 29 1/2 days, roughly 4 weeks. The four main phases come about 1 week apart: new moon, first quarter, full moon, last quarter. So from first quarter to full moon is about 1 week.

misconceptions.1: About 2 weeks is the time from new moon to full moon. First quarter is already halfway there.
misconceptions.2: This counts the wrong way round the cycle. After first quarter the Moon goes to waxing gibbous and then full moon, which is about 1 week.
misconceptions.3: About 4 weeks (29 1/2 days) is the whole cycle, from one full moon to the next.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the statements that are true about the phases of the Moon.
options: The Moon changes shape because clouds cover parts of it
Half of the Moon is always lit by the Sun
The Moon actually gets smaller when it is waning
We see different amounts of the Moon's lit half as it orbits the Earth
Full moon happens when the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun
questions.solution: The Sun always lights half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits the Earth, we see different amounts of that lit half. When the Moon is on the opposite side of the Earth from the Sun, we see all of the lit half: a full moon. The Moon's real size does not change.

misconceptions.0: Clouds can hide the Moon, but they do not cause its phases. The phases happen even on perfectly clear nights.
misconceptions.2: The Moon's size never changes. Only the amount of its lit half that we can see changes.

questions.prompt: In the old geocentric model of the universe, what was at the centre?
options: The Earth
The Sun
The Moon
The stars
questions.solution: 'Geo' means Earth. In the geocentric model, the Earth was at the centre and the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all moved around it. It matched what people saw from the ground, but later evidence showed it was wrong.

misconceptions.1: A model with the Sun at the centre is the heliocentric model. 'Geo' means Earth, so the geocentric model has the Earth at the centre.
misconceptions.2: No model put the Moon at the centre. In the geocentric model the Moon, Sun and planets all moved around the Earth.
misconceptions.3: In the geocentric model the stars were thought to be on a far-away sphere turning around the Earth, not at the centre.

questions.prompt: True or false: Long ago, many people believed that the Sun moved around the Earth, because that is how it looks from the ground.
questions.solution: True. From the ground, the Earth feels still and the Sun seems to cross the sky each day. So for a very long time most people believed in a geocentric (Earth-centred) model. New evidence later changed scientists' minds.

misconceptions.common: Thinking people long ago were just careless. They used the evidence they had; better evidence, such as telescope observations, came later.

questions.prompt: Which scientist is famous for describing a model of the Solar System with the Sun at the centre, in a book published in 1543?
options: Ptolemy
Isaac Newton
Nicolaus Copernicus
Neil Armstrong
questions.solution: Nicolaus Copernicus described a heliocentric (Sun-centred) model in 1543. Later, Galileo's telescope observations gave evidence that supported it. This shows how scientific ideas change when new evidence is found.

misconceptions.0: Ptolemy, who lived in ancient times, described the Earth-centred (geocentric) model, the one Copernicus argued against.
misconceptions.1: Newton lived later (born 1643) and is famous for explaining gravity, not for first putting the Sun at the centre.
misconceptions.3: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon, in 1969. He did not create a model of the Solar System.

questions.prompt: Your class makes a model using a lamp for the Sun, a large ball for the Earth and a small ball for the Moon. What is this model most useful for showing?
options: How the Sun lights half of the Moon, and why we see different phases as the Moon moves around the Earth
The real distances between the Sun, the Earth and the Moon
That the Moon makes its own light
How hot the Sun really is
questions.solution: Models help us understand things that are too big or too far away to see directly. With a lamp and balls, you can see that half of the 'Moon' is always lit, and that you see a different amount of that lit half as it moves around the 'Earth'. But a model is never perfect: this one does not show real sizes or distances.

misconceptions.1: In a classroom model the distances are far too small. The real Sun is about 150 million km from Earth, so this model cannot show true distances.
misconceptions.2: In the model the small ball only shines where the lamp lights it, which shows the Moon reflects light; it does not make its own.
misconceptions.3: A lamp cannot show the Sun's real temperature. The model is for showing positions, movement and lighting.

questions.prompt: In a scale model, the Earth is a ball 1 cm wide. The Sun's diameter is about 109 times the Earth's diameter. How wide should the model Sun be? Give your answer in cm.
questions.solution: The model must keep the same scale for both. 1 cm x 109 = 109 cm. That is more than a metre wide, while the Earth is the size of a pea!

misconceptions.common: Thinking the Sun only needs to be a bit bigger than the Earth because they look similar in size in pictures. Multiply the Earth's model size by 109.

questions.prompt: What name is given to a model of the Solar System that has the Sun at the centre? Answer in one word.
questions.solution: A Sun-centred model is called heliocentric. 'Helios' is the Greek word for the Sun. The Earth-centred model is called geocentric.

misconceptions.common: Answering 'geocentric'. Geo means Earth; the geocentric model has the Earth at the centre.

questions.prompt: In 1610, Galileo looked at Jupiter through a telescope and saw four moons travelling around Jupiter. Why was this important evidence against the geocentric model?
options: It proved that Jupiter is at the centre of the Solar System
It showed that Jupiter is bigger than the Sun
It proved that the Earth has four moons
It showed that not everything in the sky orbits the Earth
questions.solution: The geocentric model said that everything in the sky went around the Earth. Galileo saw moons going around Jupiter instead. That was evidence that the Earth is not the centre of everything, which supported Copernicus's Sun-centred model. New evidence changed scientific ideas.

misconceptions.0: Moons orbiting Jupiter do not put Jupiter at the centre of the Solar System. They only show that the Earth is not the centre of every orbit.
misconceptions.1: The moons tell us nothing about Jupiter being bigger than the Sun, and in fact the Sun is far bigger.
misconceptions.2: These four moons go around Jupiter, not the Earth. The Earth has only one moon.

questions.prompt: Why is it very hard to make a classroom model of the Solar System in which both the sizes of the planets and the distances between them are to the same scale?
options: The planets are close together, so they would overlap in the model
The distances are huge compared with the sizes, so either the planets would be tiny dots or the model would be far too big for the room
Scientists do not know how far away the planets are
The Sun is smaller than the planets, so it would be too hard to see
questions.solution: Real distances are enormous. If the Earth were a 1 cm ball, the Sun would be about 109 cm wide and about 117 m away, and Neptune would be about 3.5 km away! So a classroom model must choose: show sizes to scale OR distances to scale, not both. Knowing what a model cannot show is part of using models well.

misconceptions.0: Pictures and posters often show the planets close together, but in reality the gaps between them are enormous compared with their sizes.
misconceptions.2: Scientists know the distances to the planets very accurately. The problem is how huge those distances are.
misconceptions.3: The Sun is much bigger than any planet. Its diameter is about 109 times the Earth's.
